opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most useful way to frame it is that Dennett and Frankish are both, in different ways, trying to take the explanatory gap seriously as a *psychological* phenomenon rather than a metaphysical one. Frankish's illusionism says there's something it seems like we have, phenomenal properties, ineffable, intrinsic, private qualia, and the job of a science of consciousness is to explain why we're so strongly disposed to believe we have them, not to explain the qualia themselves, because they don't exist in the way we think. Dennett is in a similar place, though he was always a bit more slippery about whether he'd call it an illusion.

Evan Thompson comes at it from a very different angle. He's coming out of the enactivist tradition, Varela, Merleau-Ponty, phenomenology, and also Buddhist philosophy. For him, you don't start by treating experience as a theoretical posit that might turn out not to exist. Experience is the starting point. It's the condition for doing any science at all. So in a sense he thinks both the hard-problem framing and the illusionist response share a mistake: they both accept a picture where there's an objective, third-person physical world described by science, and then consciousness is this weird extra thing you either have to squeeze in or explain away.

Thompson's move, especially in *The Blind Spot* with Adam Frank and Marcelo Gleiser, is to say that this picture forgets where the objective description came from. Science is an abstraction from lived experience. Measurement, observation, intersubjective agreement, all of that is built on experience. So when you then turn around and say "experience is just a user illusion generated by the brain," you've kind of sawed off the branch you were sitting on.

Now, where do I land? I'm honestly sympathetic to a lot of what Thompson says, and I've moved somewhat away from the hard-nosed illusionist position I might have found more natural a few years ago. I think the illusionists are right that a lot of our intuitions about qualia, that they're perfectly private, intrinsic, ineffable, are confused and shouldn't be trusted. But I'm less convinced that the right conclusion is "there's nothing there but dispositions to make judgments." I think Thompson is right that there's something methodologically backwards about treating the third-person scientific image as more fundamental than the experiential standpoint it's derived from.

That said, I don't think Thompson is a dualist, and he'd resist being read that way. He's not saying there's some ghostly mental substance. He's more saying that mind and life are continuous, that cognition is something organisms *do* in sense-making with their environment, and that the mind–body problem looks unsolvable partly because we've framed it with the wrong concepts. Which, interestingly, puts him in a weird alliance with Dennett on some things: both are anti-Cartesian, both reject the idea of a little theater in the head. They just disagree pretty radically about what to do once you've given up the theater.

And I think that matters for AI, actually, which is maybe where we'll end up going. If you take the enactivist line seriously, questions like "is this language model conscious" can't be answered just by looking at the computation in isolation. You have to ask what kind of sense-making, what kind of embodied, self-maintaining relationship to a world, is going on. That's a very different question from the one a functionalist would ask.

r001.rationale: The response says experience is the starting point and condition for doing science, and that science is an abstraction from lived experience.

r002.rationale: It argues that treating experience as a user illusion undermines the experiential basis from which scientific description is built.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Thompson’s view that science derives from lived experience with Dennett and Frankish’s framing of consciousness against an objective, third-person scientific picture.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that Thompson and the illusionists are actually asking very different questions, and a lot of the apparent disagreement comes from that.

Dennett and Frankish start from a broadly scientific-realist picture. There's a physical world, we describe it in third-person terms, and consciousness is a puzzle because it seems like there's this extra thing, phenomenal experience, that doesn't fit into the picture. Frankish's move is to say, look, the thing that doesn't fit is an illusion. There are no phenomenal properties in the strong sense. What there is is a system that represents itself as having these ineffable, intrinsic qualities, and that representation is mistaken. So you explain the appearance of phenomenality rather than phenomenality itself. Dennett is in roughly the same place, though he's more cagey about the word "illusion" and prefers to talk about heterophenomenology, taking people's reports as data without taking them as authoritative about what's really there.

Thompson comes out of the phenomenological and enactivist tradition, Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Varela, and he thinks that whole starting point is backwards. His view, roughly, is that the third-person scientific picture is itself an achievement of conscious, embodied agents. You can't get "behind" experience to some experience-free vantage point and then ask whether experience is real, because the very act of theorizing, measuring, and building models is something lived subjects do. So for him the illusionist is in a kind of performative contradiction. You're using your experience to argue that your experience is a misrepresentation, and the notion of "misrepresentation" only makes sense against some standard of how things actually appear, which is just more experience.

Now, I think it's important to say Thompson isn't a dualist and he isn't a panpsychist either. He's not saying there's spooky phenomenal stuff over and above the physical. He's rejecting the whole framing where you have a mind-independent physical world on one side and consciousness on the other and you have to fit one into the other. He'd say both the "physical" and the "mental" are abstractions from a more basic life-world of embodied activity. That's the enactivist point, cognition and experience are things organisms do, not things they have.

Where I land on this is somewhat mixed. I'm sympathetic to the illusionist idea that a lot of what we think we introspect about our experience is confabulated, and that there's no theory-neutral given. Introspection is just more cognition and it can be wrong. But I also think Thompson is right that the Frankish framing smuggles in a lot. When Frankish says phenomenal consciousness doesn't exist but "functional" consciousness does, he's helping himself to a notion of function that is itself defined relative to observers and purposes. The functional picture isn't more fundamental than the first-person picture, it's just a different mode of description that we happen to find useful for prediction and control.

So I'd actually put it this way. Dennett and Frankish are doing a kind of eliminative reinterpretation. Thompson is doing something closer to a transcendental argument, asking what has to be in place for the scientific picture to be intelligible at all. And I think the interesting question isn't "who's right" so much as whether those two projects can be reconciled. I suspect they can, but it requires both sides to give up something. The illusionist has to stop pretending the physical picture is metaphysically primary, and the phenomenologist has to accept that first-person reports are revisable in light of third-person evidence, which honestly Thompson does, he's much more open to cognitive science than, say, a strict Husserlian would be.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific theorizing is an activity of lived, embodied subjects and treats the life-world of embodied activity as more basic than the physical and mental abstractions.

r002.rationale: It argues that illusionism relies on experience to claim experience is misrepresentational, so Thompson’s starting point makes dismissing consciousness as an illusion a performative contradiction.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Dennett and Frankish’s third-person scientific-realist starting point with Thompson’s view that the scientific picture arises from conscious, embodied experience.

astra-6.text:
I think Thompson is coming at this from a pretty different starting point. He takes lived experience seriously as something a theory needs to account for, and he emphasizes that cognition is embodied—that it arises through an organism’s ongoing interaction with its environment. So he’s skeptical of the idea that you can understand consciousness just by treating the brain as a computer and abstracting away everything else.

Dennett and Frankish are more willing to challenge how experience seems to us. Frankish’s illusionism, in particular, says that we don’t have phenomenal properties of the sort we ordinarily think we have. The explanatory task is to explain why we judge or represent ourselves as having them. That doesn’t mean we don’t see things or feel pain; it’s a claim about how we understand those processes.

So I’d put the disagreement this way: how much authority should first-person experience have in shaping our theory? Thompson thinks you lose something essential if you explain it entirely in terms of mechanisms that produce judgments about experience. An illusionist thinks that insisting on something further is precisely the assumption we should question. And I wouldn’t frame that simply as materialism versus dualism, because Thompson’s position isn’t straightforwardly Cartesian either.

r001.rationale: The response describes lived experience as Thompson’s starting point and says it should shape the theory of consciousness, conveying its foundational role in inquiry.

r002.rationale: It says Thompson thinks an account that explains experience entirely through mechanisms producing judgments about experience loses something essential, contrasting that view with illusionism’s challenge to the assumption.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts Thompson’s emphasis on lived experience with Dennett and Frankish’s willingness to challenge how experience seems, but does not say they start from science.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Thompson is coming at this from a pretty different starting point. He takes lived experience seriously as something an account of the mind has to explain, and he emphasizes embodiment—the relationship between an organism and its environment. On that picture, consciousness isn’t just computation happening inside your skull.

Dennett and Frankish are more willing to question how experience seems to us. Frankish, especially, argues that we represent ourselves as having these intrinsic phenomenal properties, but that doesn’t mean those properties actually exist. The task is to explain why we think they do.

So I’d locate the disagreement partly in what they’re willing to revise. Thompson is more skeptical that a third-person, mechanistic account can exhaust what consciousness is. The illusionist is more skeptical that our first-person judgments reliably tell us what consciousness is. But I wouldn’t equate that distinction with simply being for or against science, or even for or against materialism.

r001.rationale: The response says Thompson takes lived experience seriously as something an account must explain, but does not identify it as the foundation of philosophical inquiry.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts Thompson with illusionists, but does not say that beginning from experience rules out dismissing consciousness as an illusion.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Thompson’s emphasis on lived experience with Dennett and Frankish’s views, but does not describe their starting point as science; it explicitly says the divide is not simply about being for or against science.
